contribution: Heat and work are two ways of transferring energy into or out of a system, and their sum is the change in the internal energy of the system: $\Delta U = Q + W$, the first law of thermodynamics. Heat is a transfer of energy; internal energy is a property of the system.
learn: You distinguish heat, work and internal energy: heat and work transfer energy, while internal energy is a property of the system.
You can apply the first law of thermodynamics.
prior: Work $W = Fs$ transfers energy, and in Joule's experiment work heated water (chapter *Work and energy*)
Micro model of a gas: temperature tells you the average kinetic energy of the particles (chapter *Thermodynamic system, state variables and temperature*)

activities.text: You pump a bicycle tyre to a high pressure. At the end, the lower end of the pump, where the air is compressed, feels warm in your hand. After the pump has rested for a while, it is at room temperature again. On the other hand, when you let air out of the tyre through the valve, the valve feels cool, even though nothing is cooling it.
activities.question: Where does the air in the pump get extra energy if it is not heated, and where does that energy go when the pump cools down?

activities.title: Review: the micro model of temperature
activities.prompt: In chapter *Thermodynamic system, state variables and temperature*, the temperature of a gas was described with a micro model. What happens to the particles of a gas when its temperature rises?

choices.text: The particles expand and take up more space.
choices.feedback: In the micro model, the size of the particles does not change with temperature. Temperature tells you about the motion of the particles: their average kinetic energy.

choices.text: The average kinetic energy of the particles increases.
choices.feedback: Correct: according to the micro model, temperature tells you the average kinetic energy of the particles. A higher temperature means faster-moving particles.

choices.text: More particles enter the gas.
choices.feedback: The amount of substance is a state variable of its own. The temperature can rise even though the number of particles stays the same; then the same particles move faster on average.

choices.text: Each particle itself becomes hotter.
choices.feedback: A single particle does not have a temperature. Temperature describes the average kinetic energy of a large group of particles.

activities.title: Prediction 1: why does compressed air get hot?
activities.prompt: Three students explain why the air in a pump gets hot when the piston is pushed quickly down and the nozzle is blocked. Whose explanation do you think is best? Justify your choice briefly.

choices.text: Aino: When the air is compressed, its pressure increases. The particles hit the walls more often, and the high pressure raises the temperature of the air.
choices.feedback: In the conducting cylinder of experiment 2, the air was compressed to $75\,\%$ of the volume and its pressure increased to 1.33 times the original, but the temperature returned to $293\,\text{K}$. So high pressure alone does not make a gas hot. What decides the rise in temperature is how much energy stays in the gas.

choices.text: Bea: The piston does work on the air. Work transfers energy to the air, so the internal energy of the air increases and its temperature rises.
choices.feedback: The experiments support this. In the insulated cylinder, the work of the piston $W \approx +13.1\,\text{J}$ stayed entirely in the gas ($\Delta U = W$), and the temperature rose by about $37\,\text{K}$. Look at a particle that hits the moving piston: it bounces off faster. In a real pump, friction between the piston and the cylinder also heats it a little; there is no friction in the simulation.

choices.text: Cem: The air contains a certain amount of heat. When it is compressed, the same heat is packed into a smaller space, so the air feels hotter.
choices.feedback: This explanation treats heat as a substance of which the air contains a certain amount. Then the same compression would always heat by the same amount. In experiment 2 the compression was the same both times, but in the insulated cylinder the temperature rose by about $37\,\text{K}$, while in the conducting one it returned to $293\,\text{K}$, because a quantity of heat of about $12\,\text{J}$ was transferred out through the walls.

activities.title: Prediction 2: a fast or a slow push?
activities.prompt: The walls of the cylinder in the simulation are insulated, so no heat is transferred. The piston is pushed to the same position twice: once slowly and once quickly. What decides which time the temperature of the gas rises more?

choices.text: The speed of the piston itself: fast motion heats the gas even if the work is the same.
choices.feedback: In the model readings, the fast push heated more ($\Delta T$ about $53\,\text{K}$, the slow one $37\,\text{K}$), but the work was also greater: $19.1\,\text{J}$ and $13.1\,\text{J}$. When you divide $\Delta T$ by the work, you get about $2.8\,\text{K/J}$ for both. The speed matters only through the work: the temperature rose exactly as much as the work done.

choices.text: The number of pushes: in a slow push the particles have time to hit the piston more often, so the gas warms more.
choices.feedback: In a slow push there are more hits, but each hit speeds the particle up less. In the model readings the slow push heated less: $\Delta T$ about $37\,\text{K}$ and $W = +13.1\,\text{J}$, the fast one $53\,\text{K}$ and $+19.1\,\text{J}$. The rise in temperature followed the work.

choices.text: The distance of the push alone: the distance is the same, so the work and the rise in temperature are exactly the same.
choices.feedback: The distance was the same, but the work was not: for the slow push $W = +13.1\,\text{J}$, for the fast one $+19.1\,\text{J}$. Work is force times distance, and the particles hit a fast piston at a greater relative speed, so the gas resists it with a greater force. That is why the temperature also rose more with the fast push, $53\,\text{K}$ instead of $37\,\text{K}$.

choices.text: The work done: in an insulated cylinder the internal energy increases by the amount of the work ($\Delta U = W$), so the gas warms more the time more work is done.
choices.feedback: The model readings support this. With the slow push $W = \Delta U = +13.1\,\text{J}$ and $\Delta T$ about $37\,\text{K}$, with the fast push $W = \Delta U = +19.1\,\text{J}$ and $\Delta T$ about $53\,\text{K}$. The particles hit a fast piston at a greater relative speed, so the gas resists it more and the work increases. The rise in temperature per unit of work is about $2.8\,\text{K/J}$ in both cases: the speed matters only through the work.

choices.text: Neither: the temperature does not rise either time, because no heat enters the insulated cylinder.
choices.feedback: The temperature rose both times, even though $Q = 0$. Work also increases the internal energy: the work of the piston stayed entirely in the gas, $\Delta U = W$.

activities.text: The simulation has a cylinder with 40 gas particles and a piston. Try it freely, including pulling the piston out.
activities.howto: *Push the piston* compresses the gas to $75\,\%$ of the volume, and *Pull out* returns the piston. The colour of a particle shows its speed. When a particle hits the moving piston, it briefly gets a long trail and a green ring: it bounces off faster. The bars show the work $W$ done by the piston on the gas, the quantity of heat $Q$ transferred into the gas through the walls and the change in internal energy $\Delta U$. *Piston speed* chooses a slow or a fast push, *Walls* insulated or conducting walls, and *Animation* only the pace: it does not change the readings. The model is completely repeatable, because a push from the initial state always starts from the same state of the gas.
activities.model: The numbers are values from the model, not measurements from a real pump. The gas in the model corresponds to $0.50\,\text{g}$ of air: its internal energy increases by $0.359\,\text{J}$ for each kelvin. The gas has $40$ particles that move in a plane and do not collide with each other. Air molecules also rotate, so each particle has rotational energy in addition to kinetic energy, which the picture does not show. A fixed wall sends a particle that hits it off in a random direction and redistributes its energy between motion and rotation; an insulated wall does not change the total energy of the particle. In this way the gas stays in equilibrium, and a slow insulated push corresponds to a slow compression of air without heat transfer. For this, physics gives $T_2 = T_1 (V_1/V_2)^{\gamma - 1} = 293\,\text{K} \cdot (4/3)^{0.4} \approx 329\,\text{K}$, when $\gamma \approx 1.4$ for air; the simulation gives $330\,\text{K}$. The small difference is mainly because there are only $40$ particles: with another random initial state the work would vary by about $11$–$15\,\text{J}$. In a real pump the piston is much slower than the molecules (about $500\,\text{m/s}$), so there the difference arises mainly from whether heat has time to be transferred out.
activities.calc: A particle that hits the piston bounces off like a ball off a bat: if the piston moves towards it at speed $u$, the speed of the particle in the direction of the piston increases by $2u$, $v_x' = 2u - v_x$. The work $W$ of the piston is the kinetic energy the particles gain in this way, equal to the force of the piston times the distance. When the piston is pulled out, the particles bounce off slower and $W$ is negative. In an insulated cylinder $Q = 0$ and $\Delta U = W$. A conducting wall is at room temperature $293\,\text{K}$: a particle that hits it bounces off with less energy if the gas is warmer than the room, and with more if the gas is colder. The energy transferred in this way is the quantity of heat $Q$, and $\Delta U = Q + W$. The slow piston moves about $50$ times slower than the particles on average, the fast one only about $3.5$ times slower. The particles hit a fast piston at a greater relative speed, and the energy does not have time to spread evenly, so the gas resists the piston more and over the same distance the work is greater; in an insulated cylinder the temperature rises by exactly as much more as the work, $\Delta T = W/C$. The temperature is calculated from the total energy of the particles and the pressure $p/p_0$ from the temperature and the volume.

activities.title: Experiment 1: only the piston speed changes
activities.intro: Test prediction 2. The walls are locked as insulated, and only the speed of the piston changes. In the simulation press *To the start* and *Push the piston*. When the piston has stopped ($V = 75\,\%$), press *Record measurement*. Then change the speed of the piston, press *To the start* and *Push the piston* again, and record again. Compare, for both runs, the change in internal energy $\Delta U$ and the work $W$ and the temperature rise $\Delta T$. A slow push takes about $19\,\text{s}$; *Animation: fast* speeds up the viewing without changing the readings.

activities.title: Experiment 2: only the walls change
activities.intro: Test prediction 1. The speed of the piston is locked to slow, and only the walls change. First do the push in an insulated cylinder (*To the start*, *Push the piston*) and record when the piston has stopped. Then change the walls to conducting, press *To the start* and *Push the piston*. When the piston has stopped, wait until $T$ is about $293\,\text{K}$, and only then record. Also watch the bars: the bar pointing up is energy that has entered the gas, the bar pointing down is energy that has left the gas.

question.prompt: Look at the measurement for the conducting wall and at the bars when the temperature has returned to $293\,\text{K}$. Which description fits the bars?

choices.text: $W$ points up, $Q$ is equally long pointing down, and $\Delta U$ is almost zero.
choices.feedback: Correct. The work of the piston brought about $12.4\,\text{J}$ into the gas, and an equal amount of energy left as heat through the walls, so $Q \approx -12.4\,\text{J}$ and $\Delta U = Q + W \approx 0$. A bar pointing up is positive, that is, energy that came into the gas, and a bar pointing down is negative, that is, energy that left the gas.

choices.text: $W$ points up, $Q$ is zero, and $\Delta U$ is equal to $W$.
choices.feedback: This is what happened in the insulated cylinder. In the conducting cylinder the bar of $Q$ pointed down, about $-12.4\,\text{J}$, because energy was transferred from the hot gas to the walls.

choices.text: $W$ and $Q$ both point up, and $\Delta U$ is their sum.
choices.feedback: The bar of $Q$ pointed down. Heat was transferred out of the gas, so $Q$ is negative. That is why the sum $\Delta U = Q + W$ ended up almost zero.

choices.text: All three are zero, because the temperature did not change in the end.
choices.feedback: $\Delta U$ is almost zero, but the piston still did work $W \approx +12.4\,\text{J}$. The energy passed through the gas: it came in as work and left as heat.

activities.title: Conclusion: what increases internal energy?
activities.prompt: Write a short conclusion based on your tables. How did the rise in temperature depend on the work done in the insulated cylinder? Where did the energy brought by the work go in the conducting cylinder? Which of the explanations in prediction 1 do your measurements refute, and with which readings?
activities.model: In the insulated cylinder, the temperature rose the more, the more work the piston did: with the slow push $W = +13.1\,\text{J}$ and $\Delta T \approx 37\,\text{K}$, with the fast push $W = +19.1\,\text{J}$ and $\Delta T \approx 53\,\text{K}$, in both cases about $2.8\,\text{K}$ per joule. All the work stayed in the gas, $\Delta U = W$. In the conducting cylinder the same compression did work $W \approx +12.4\,\text{J}$, but an equal amount of energy left as heat through the walls, $Q \approx -12.4\,\text{J}$, and the temperature returned to $293\,\text{K}$, even though the pressure remained $1.33$ times the original. So Aino's explanation (pressure raises the temperature) and Cem's explanation (heat is packed together) do not hold: the same compression gave a different temperature depending on whether the energy stayed in the gas. The readings are calculated by the model; with a real pump you could measure the same with a thermometer.
criteria: I linked the rise in temperature to the work done, using numbers.
I said that in the conducting cylinder the energy brought by the work left as heat ($Q \approx -W$).
I used a measurement to justify why high pressure or "packed-together heat" does not explain the warming.
I used the concepts work, heat and internal energy correctly.

activities.title: Back to your predictions
activities.prompt: Compare your predictions with the experiments and with the model $\Delta U = Q + W$. Then return to the question at the start: where does the air in the pump get extra energy, and where does the energy go when the pump cools down? Why does air escaping from the valve feel cool? You can try in the simulation what happens when the piston is pulled out.

activities.title: Find the error
activities.prompt: A quantity of heat of $250\,\text{J}$ is transferred into the gas in a cylinder, and the gas expands, doing $90\,\text{J}$ of work on the piston. A student calculates: $\Delta U = Q + W = 250\,\text{J} + 90\,\text{J} = 340\,\text{J}$. Where is the error?

choices.text: $Q$ should be negative, because the gas expands.
choices.feedback: $Q$ tells you the direction of the heat, not of the motion. Heat is transferred into the gas, so $Q = +250\,\text{J}$ is correct. The error is in the other term.

choices.text: The gas does work on the surroundings, so $W = -90\,\text{J}$ and $\Delta U = 250\,\text{J} - 90\,\text{J} = 160\,\text{J}$.
choices.feedback: Correct. In the formula $\Delta U = Q + W$, the work $W$ is the work done on the system by the surroundings. When the gas itself pushes the piston, energy leaves the gas, so $W$ is negative.

choices.text: Heat and work are different things, so they cannot be added together.
choices.feedback: Heat and work are two ways of transferring energy, and both are measured in joules. So they can be added together, as long as the signs give the direction correctly.

choices.text: There is no error in the calculation.
choices.feedback: Check in which direction energy is transferred as work. An expanding gas does work on the surroundings, so the work takes energy away from the gas instead of bringing it in.

activities.title: Apply to a new situation
activities.prompt: A fire piston has a closed cylinder with tinder at the bottom. The piston is pushed quickly down with the palm of the hand, and the compressed air gets so hot that the tinder ignites. The palm pushes the piston with an average force of 75 N over a distance of 8.0 cm, and during the compression a quantity of heat of $0.60\,\text{J}$ has time to be transferred from the air to the walls. By how much does the internal energy of the air increase? Assume that all the work of the palm is done on the air (ignore friction). Give the answer in joules.
hints: What is the system, and in which direction is energy transferred as work and in which as heat?
The work of the piston is $W = Fs$ with the average force, and $\Delta U = Q + W$. Heat leaving the system is negative.

mistakes.feedback: You added the quantity of heat. Heat is transferred from the air to the walls, that is, out of the system, so $Q = -0.60\,\text{J}$ and it reduces the increase in internal energy.
The distance must be converted to metres before multiplying: $8.0\,\text{cm} = 0.080\,\text{m}$, so $W = 6.0\,\text{J}$. A joule is a newton metre, $1\,\text{J} = 1\,\text{N}\cdot\text{m}$.

activities.solution:
**Given:** the system is the air in the cylinder; force of the palm $F = 75\,\text{N}$ (average), distance $s = 8.0\,\text{cm}$, heat transferred from the air to the walls $0.60\,\text{J}$; friction is ignored

**Find:** the increase in internal energy of the air $\Delta U$ in joules

**Principle:** Energy is conserved, so the change in internal energy is the sum of the heat and work transferred into the system. The piston is part of the surroundings, which do work $W = Fs$ on the air, because the force and the displacement are in the same direction and the average force is known. Heat is transferred out of the air, so $Q$ is negative.

**Formula:**

$$\Delta U = Q + W = Q + Fs$$

**Conversions:** Distance to metres: $s = 8.0\,\text{cm} = 0.080\,\text{m}$, so that $Fs$ comes out in joules ($1\,\text{N}\cdot\text{m} = 1\,\text{J}$).

**Substitution:** $\Delta U = -0.60\,\text{J} + 75\,\text{N} \cdot 0.080\,\text{m} = -0.60\,\text{J} + 6.0\,\text{J} = 5.4\,\text{J}$

**Answer:** $5.4\,\text{J}$, two significant figures, like the data $0.60\,\text{J}$ and $8.0\,\text{cm}$.

**Reasonableness:** The compression is so fast that only a small part of the work ($0.60\,\text{J}$, or $10\,\%$ of $6.0\,\text{J}$) has time to be transferred out, so $\Delta U$ is close to the work of $6.0\,\text{J}$ and positive. A few joules are enough to heat the small amount of air in the cylinder to the ignition temperature of the tinder. If no heat were transferred, the result would be $6.0\,\text{J}$.

activities.text: Practise some more on three levels. For level 1 tasks, $\Delta U = Q + W$ and the correct signs are enough; level 3 requires reasoning.

activities.title: 1. Concept
activities.prompt: A gas expands in a very well insulated cylinder and pushes the piston outwards. No heat is transferred into or out of the gas. What happens to the temperature of the gas?

choices.text: It stays the same, because no heat is transferred.
choices.feedback: Internal energy is changed by work as well as by heat. The gas does work on the piston, so $W < 0$ and $\Delta U = Q + W < 0$, even though $Q = 0$.

choices.text: It falls, because the gas does work and its internal energy decreases.
choices.feedback: Correct. $Q = 0$ and $W < 0$, so $\Delta U = Q + W < 0$. A smaller internal energy means that the particles move more slowly on average and the temperature falls. This is why air escaping from the valve feels cool.

choices.text: It rises, because the particles move faster in an expanding gas.
choices.feedback: The particles of an expanding gas bounce off a piston moving away more slowly than they hit it. Energy is transferred from the gas to the piston, so the internal energy decreases.

activities.title: 2. Heat and internal energy
activities.prompt: A stone heated in a campfire is put into cold water. Which statement describes the situation correctly?

choices.text: A hot stone has a lot of heat in it, and the heat is transferred from the stone to the water.
choices.feedback: This sounds natural, but heat is not a property of an object that is stored in the stone. The stone has internal energy and a high temperature. Heat is a transfer of energy, and it exists only while the transfer is happening.

choices.text: The stone has a higher temperature than the water, so energy is transferred from the stone to the water as heat. The internal energy of the stone decreases and that of the water increases.
choices.feedback: Correct. A temperature difference makes energy transfer from the hotter object to the colder one, and this transferred energy is called heat. The internal energy of the stone decreases and that of the water increases, and energy is conserved.

choices.text: When the stone and the water reach the same temperature, the heat has disappeared.
choices.feedback: Energy does not disappear. The energy given up by the stone has ended up in the water and increased its internal energy. Once the temperatures have evened out, no more heat is transferred, but there is still as much energy as at the start.

choices.text: Temperature is transferred from the stone to the water until the temperatures are equal.
choices.feedback: Temperature is not transferred anywhere. It measures the average kinetic energy of the particles. The quantity that is transferred is energy, called heat, and as a result the temperature of the stone falls and that of the water rises.

activities.title: 3. Energy bookkeeping
activities.prompt: The gas in a cylinder goes through two stages. In stage 1 the piston compresses the gas, doing $80\,\text{J}$ of work on it, and a quantity of heat of $30\,\text{J}$ is transferred from the gas to the walls. In stage 2 a quantity of heat of $50\,\text{J}$ is transferred into the gas, and the gas expands, doing $70\,\text{J}$ of work on the piston. By how much does the internal energy of the gas change during the two stages in total? Give the answer in joules.
hints: Write $Q$ and $W$ with their signs for each stage: does the energy come into the system or leave it?
In stage 1 $Q_1 = -30\,\text{J}$ and $W_1 = +80\,\text{J}$, in stage 2 $Q_2 = +50\,\text{J}$ and $W_2 = -70\,\text{J}$.
$\Delta U_1 = 50\,\text{J}$ and $\Delta U_2 = -20\,\text{J}$. Add them together.

mistakes.feedback: You counted all the transfers as positive. Energy leaving the system is negative: the heat transferred to the walls ($-30\,\text{J}$) and the work of the expanding gas ($-70\,\text{J}$).
You used the wrong sign for the work. In this book $W$ is the work done on the system by the surroundings: in compression $W_1 = +80\,\text{J}$, in expansion $W_2 = -70\,\text{J}$.

activities.solution:
**Given:** the system is the gas in the cylinder; stage 1: $W_1 = +80\,\text{J}$ (the piston does work on the gas), $Q_1 = -30\,\text{J}$ (heat to the walls); stage 2: $Q_2 = +50\,\text{J}$, $W_2 = -70\,\text{J}$ (the gas does work on the piston)

**Find:** the total change in internal energy $\Delta U$ in joules

**Principle:** Energy is conserved, so in both stages $\Delta U = Q + W$. Changes in internal energy are energy, so they can be added together: the total change is the sum of the changes of the stages. Energy into the system is positive and energy out of the system is negative.

**Formula:**

$$\begin{aligned}
&\Delta U = \Delta U_1 + \Delta U_2 \\
&= (Q_1 + W_1) \\
&\quad + (Q_2 + W_2)
\end{aligned}$$

**Conversions:** None needed: all energies are given in joules.

**Substitution:** $\Delta U_1 = -30\,\text{J} + 80\,\text{J} = 50\,\text{J}$ and $\Delta U_2 = 50\,\text{J} + (-70\,\text{J}) = -20\,\text{J}$. So $\Delta U = 50\,\text{J} + (-20\,\text{J}) = 30\,\text{J}$

**Answer:** $30\,\text{J}$, two significant figures, because all the transfers are given in whole joules.

**Reasonableness:** Add up all the transfers at once: $80\,\text{J} + 50\,\text{J} = 130\,\text{J}$ came in and $30\,\text{J} + 70\,\text{J} = 100\,\text{J}$ went out, so $130\,\text{J} - 100\,\text{J} = 30\,\text{J}$ stayed in the gas. The result is positive because more came in than went out, and the gas warms up.

activities.title: 4. Explain and transfer
activities.prompt: You pump the same tyre twice to the same pressure: once quickly and once very slowly. Both times you do roughly the same amount of work on the air. Explain why the pump gets warmer when you pump quickly. Use the concepts internal energy, work and heat, and the equation $\Delta U = Q + W$.
criteria: I say that work transfers energy to the air and increases its internal energy, which shows up as a rise in temperature.
I say that energy is transferred as heat from the warm air through the walls to the surroundings, so $Q$ is negative.
I explain that in slow pumping more heat has time to be transferred out, so $\Delta U = Q + W$ remains smaller.
I distinguish heat (a transfer of energy) from internal energy (the energy of the system).
activities.model: The work $W$ of the piston transfers energy to the air, and the internal energy of the air increases: the particles move faster on average, and the temperature rises. When the air is warmer than the surroundings, energy is transferred from it as heat through the walls to the surroundings, so $Q$ is negative. In fast pumping only a little heat has time to be transferred, so $\Delta U = Q + W$ is almost equal to the work and the air gets very hot. In slow pumping almost all the energy brought by the work has time to be transferred out as heat, so $Q \approx -W$, the internal energy increases only a little and the pump hardly warms up. Energy is not lost in either case: it ends up as internal energy of the surroundings.

activities.text: Finally, two quick questions. Answer first by yourself, and only then open the answer.
